fullText:
As millennials return to the games of their youth, remakes of Star Fox and Halo suggest there is still plenty to learn from the past

Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? 
As much as some people more or less cease to listen to new music in their 30s, I have noticed a retreat to safe, familiar gaming territory among some of my fellow millennial gamers.

Retro collections are started, or resumed; jewel-cases of PS1 classics or cardboard boxes with SNES or Mega Drive games have started to colonise the living-room shelves. People are replaying things from their university days, or sticking to comfort games such as Stardew Valley. Many of the friends I used to game with never bothered to pick up a PlayStation 5 at its launch, and now that current-generation consoles are becoming prohibitively expensive, they see no need. With thousands of great older games, why bother playing something new?

My job, and an insatiable desire for novelty, has kept me in constant contact with new games, but nonetheless, I have been spending a lot of time lately with the titles I played in my youth because people keep remaking them. Lylat Wars (N64, 1997) and Halo: Combat Evolved (Xbox, 2001) have both had summer 2026 glow-ups, in the form of Star Fox on Switch 2 and Halo: Campaign Evolved on the other consoles and PC. These are games I played for many, many hours back in the day, and I remembered them beat for beat (or so I thought – it turns out I did not remember how to navigate the deadly lava planet that ended my first Star Fox run).

I was not enormously enthused by the prospect of either remake, because I’d rather play an original game in either of these series than rehash my rose-tinted recollections from 25 years ago (let’s just gloss over how old that makes us feel, shall we?). But, it turns out all those years have given me a fresh perspective. Both of these remakes are very good. And not just because I played them at the time and remember them fondly, but because each of them does things that new video games don’t. They feel novel, because in 2026, they are.

When was the last time you played an arcadey on-rails space shooter? When was the last time you enjoyed an atmospheric single-player FPS with intelligent computer-controlled enemies? These genres have fallen out of fashion – space games are now wide-open exploreathons such as No Man’s Sky (which celebrates its 10th anniversary this week), and multiplayer shooters have crowded single-player ones out almost entirely. In this context, Star Fox and Halo feel fresh. They’re not awkward transplants from another time.

Neither game really needed all that much massaging. Velan Studios in New York, entrusted with a characterful if visually basic Nintendo 64 shooter, has changed almost nothing about it: we fly through the same webbed map of planets, with the same enemies and bosses, firing off the same simple yet effective lasers and bombs and flight manoeuvres. A Star Fox playthrough takes maybe 60 to 90 minutes and you can play it over and over, like a generous arcade cabinet. In reconstructing the game, Velan has made it look very beautiful, spliced in some new cutscenes and dialogue, and added multiplayer and challenge modes that give some structure to your replays, but quite miraculously, it barely feels different. And it’s great.

Halo: Campaign Evolved deviates more from Bungie’s original space opera. It’s been rebuilt in Unreal Engine 5 with different vehicle handling and more overwrought cutscenes. But the essentials remain: high drama, perfect weaponry, and intelligent enemies that react interestingly to how you play, diving out of the way of fire or ordering a change of tactics. I never minded dying, because each firefight would be different on every playthrough. I still hate the Flood – the mindless zombies that infect the game from the midway point onwards – but despite their unwelcome incursion, I had a blast playing through this game again with my partner. I haven’t played a better co-op multiplayer game than the original Halo in all the years since, which is honestly quite sad.

I have no desire for things to return to the way they were in the late 90s and early 00s; despite its expansion and consequent unwelcome corporatisation as a business, gaming as an art form is far broader and more interesting now than it was then. But these remakes show there are things to be learned from the games of the past, and a lot that is enviable about their design philosophy. Old games don’t necessarily need to be fixed to be appreciated anew. Refreshing them is often enough.

I truly thought I was done with Pokémon Pokopia, having spent 40 hours with it back in March. When I downloaded the new expansion – an underwater area called Bubbly Basin, which turns out to be the ruins of Cerulean City, home to Misty from Pokémon Red/Blue – I did not expect to be consumed by it yet again. The rhythm and purpose of this game is just so comforting: explore, restore, revive. I have enjoyed it so much that I went back to the rest of the game with new enthusiasm for attracting new Pokémon and rebuilding the ruined planet that humans left behind for them.

Available on: Nintendo Switch 2

 Estimated playtime: 10+ hours

Rockstar Games will finally show off more of Grand Theft Auto VI on 27 August … via a broadcast on Netflix. Well, that’s new. I can only imagine the £££ exchanged for the few hours of exclusivity that the streaming giant will enjoy.

The Washington Post’s Gene Park spent some time with The Weeknd, who has been documenting his gaming habits on an Instagram alt account – even meeting developers. He wants everyone to know about the horror fishing game he’s currently obsessed with.

Metroid turned 40 at the end of last week – and so did Samus Aran, one of the earliest female protagonists in video games. Maddy Myers writes about her personal heroine.

This week’s question comes from reader Leo:

“My wife and I are big gamers – and we’re having our first kid in September. What should my partner and I play as new parents? Is it even possible?”

I mean, anything is possible if you put your mind to it – my partner played quite a bit of Death Stranding while bouncing around the living room with our second baby strapped to him, in an unlikely case of life imitating art. But it is reasonable to downgrade your expectations for how much time, attention and energy you will have for video games when you have a new baby in the house. When my nine-year-old son was a baby, I wrote this article about how to play games when you’re an exhausted new parent, and though the specific game recommendations are a little out of date, I reckon the advice remains sound. For instance: “Anything even slightly stressful, emotional or difficult might make you cry, so leave the competitive shooters and Dark Souls runs for a while.”

title: A millennial who's tried more than 30 side hustles shares the most lucrative, the biggest flop, and the easiest way to get started
description: "There is a side hustle for everyone," said Cody Berman, who's experimented with more than 30 different ways to make money.
fullText:
Serial entrepreneur Cody Berman has tried over 30 side hustles.

He's found that scalable side hustles, like digital products and real estate, are most lucrative over time.

His advice to beginners, though, is to start with time-for-money gigs to quickly earn cash and fund bigger ventures.

Cody Berman's first entrepreneurial venture was a disc golf manufacturing company he started with a friend at 19.

The business was not a financial home run, the now 30-year-old told Business Insider, but it taught him skills he would use for years: "I learned how to market, how to network, how manufacturing works, how to talk to customers, build websites."

Over the next decade, Berman kept experimenting.

The Massachusetts-based serial entrepreneur, author of "Retire by 30," and host of "The FI Show" had a brief stint in the corporate world, working about seven months in commercial real estate lending. During that time, he lived on side-hustle income and saved his full salary, building a roughly $35,000 cushion that gave him the confidence to quit corporate and pursue entrepreneurship full time.

Since then, Berman said, he has tried more than 30 side hustles. The ones that worked best helped him reach financial independence in his mid-20s.

Berman thinks of side hustles in four categories: trading time for money, scalable income streams, sharing-economy plays, and hybrid or agency-style businesses. The ones that have been most lucrative for him fall into the second category, which he calls "type two" side hustles.

These are scalable income streams that can keep earning after the initial work is done. Or, as he puts it, "something that is going to pay me in perpetuity," such as a digital product, blog post, podcast episode, YouTube video, or rental property — anything that requires upfront effort but can continue producing income over time.

His top income driver today is his digital product business, Gold City Ventures. It started with Berman selling Valentine's Day-themed love coupons and notes on Etsy and has since expanded into a template library and courses, including an E-Printables side hustle course.

Real estate has become another major income stream. Having experimented with long-term rentals, Airbnbs, house hacking, flipping, and hard-money lending, Berman now focuses on real-estate syndications. His third main income bucket is personal-finance education, which includes his podcast, social media, YouTube channel, and book.

title: Gen Z and millennial professionals are avoiding phone calls — and paying a price at work
description: A self-improvement app found that 42% of surveyed Gen Zers and millennials don't answer phone calls, while 58% script or rehearse conversations.
fullText:
A new survey of 2,000 young workers by RiseGuide found that 42% avoid phone calls.

Many Gen Z and millennial workers said that their avoidance of phone calls costs them opportunities.

RiseGuide said that technology provides people "countless ways to delay real conversations."

A fear of phone calls may be costing young workers raises and career opportunities.

A new survey of 2,000 Gen Zers and millennials by the self-improvement app RiseGuide found that 42% don't answer phone calls, while 58% script or rehearse conversations before making them.

The consequences may extend beyond anxiety. Among respondents who avoid spoken conversations, 78% said the habit has cost them earnings or opportunities.

The findings come as anxiety around phone calls appears to be growing. RiseGuide coined the term "callergy" for the reluctance to speak over the phone and finding workarounds like texts, emails, and social media messages.

Jaimee Campanella, a time strategist and productivity consultant at RiseGuide, said that the convenience of technology now provides people "countless ways to delay real conversations" so that communication skills don't get to improve through practice.

"Text messages, emails, and social media give us time to edit our responses, while face-to-face communication requires us to engage in the moment," said Campanella. "The more we postpone difficult conversations, the more intimidating they can seem."

"Unfortunately, avoidance often creates bigger problems than the conversation itself," Campanella added. "We miss opportunities, strain relationships, and spend unnecessary time and energy worrying about issues that could have been resolved through a direct discussion."

The current tough job market for young workers, however, may be nudging some out of their comfort zone.

Adrian Poon, a Gen Z HR worker trying to transition from temporary contracts to a more permanent position, told Business Insider — over text messages — that he overcomes his anxiety about answering calls only when he is "in job applying mode." He usually won't pick up unless the caller is a friend.

"I would mentally register that as a blind box opening," said Poon of getting a call from a number not in his contacts.

Poon said that although he has been actively job-seeking, he has never cold-called a recruiter and generally prefers to connect in other ways. Having a prescheduled call with a clear agenda also helps, says Poon.

"This is more of a talking to people thing in general, especially if they're busy people: I need to know what I need to ask," Poon said of calling others, including friends. "Like I figure out what I need to tell them and what I need to ask so that I don't waste my time with them."

GenZers and millennials have a complicated relationship with their devices, especially smartphones. While younger workers often prefer texting to talking, many are also trying to spend less time on their devices altogether. More people are making digital detoxes part of their lives, turning to app blockers like Brick or "dumb phones" to curb screen time.

Being more conscious of screen time doesn't necessarily mean young people are eager to pick up the phone: In RiseGuide's survey, one in 10 respondents said a spontaneous call is the most stressful form of communication for them — more than a breakup or a job interview.
